tiles.title: Resource-oriented REST URLs and CRUD contracts · FastAPI application and path-operation declarations

steps.title: The rule: Resource-oriented REST URLs and CRUD contracts

blocks.text: A URL path identifies a resource, and an HTTP method supplies the operation semantics rather than the path alone determining the action.

Model an item resource with a path parameter for its identifier and a collection resource without that item identifier. Specify retrieval with GET, collection-specific creation processing with POST, target replacement with PUT and removal with DELETE, preserving each method's semantics. A creation contract can use 201 with a Location identifying the created resource, while an absent item can use 404.

edges.label: On this item: GET retrieves; PUT replaces; DELETE removes.
POST collection creation: can use 201 + Location

blocks.alt_text: Make the orders collection and identified item visible as distinct resources. Annotate GET retrieval, POST collection creation processing, PUT item replacement and DELETE item removal, with 201 and Location /orders/42 for creation and 404 for an absent item.

steps.title: Trace the boundary: Resource-oriented REST URLs and CRUD contracts

blocks.text: Keep resource identity separate from the operation: /orders is the collection; /orders/{order_id} identifies an item. GET retrieves, POST processes collection creation, PUT replaces the target, and DELETE removes it. A creation contract can pair 201 with Location /orders/42; an absent item can use 404. Changing the method changes the semantics even when the item path stays the same.

steps.title: The rule: FastAPI application and path-operation declarations

blocks.text: Create a FastAPI instance and register a handler with @app.get("/path"), @app.post("/path"), @app.put("/path") or @app.delete("/path") for the intended method and path.

A path operation is the combination of an HTTP method and a path; handlers registered for different methods on the same path serve different operations. Routes are evaluated in order, so declare a fixed path before a conflicting parameterized path to prevent the latter from capturing it.

annotations.text: Review method, path, and declaration order together. GET and PUT on the item path register different operations. Declare /orders/current before a conflicting /orders/{order_id} route: the earlier parameterized route can capture the fixed path. A later fixed declaration does not automatically win.

An earlier conflicting /orders/{order_id} declaration can capture this request. Separately, compare @app.get and @app.put on the item path: each registers its own handler for a different operation, even with identical path text.

steps.title: The rule: Validated environment-based configuration with fail-fast startup

blocks.text: Subclass BaseSettings from pydantic_settings and declare typed fields to load and validate external configuration.

Construct Settings() to read environment variables and validate their types, with missing required settings or invalid values producing validation failures. Use SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env") as model_config when a dotenv file should provide settings; environment variables take precedence over its values.

steps.title: The rule: Async-compatible external HTTP requests

blocks.text: Choose httpx.AsyncClient and await client.get(...), client.post(...) or another request method for an asynchronous outbound call.

Reuse a scoped AsyncClient instead of creating clients inside a hot loop to benefit from connection pooling. Close a client with async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client or await client.aclose() at the end of its owning scope.

blocks.code:
import httpx

# Synthetic URLs: the exercise harness must intercept requests; never contact them.
lookup_urls = ("https://shipping.example.test/orders/42", "https://shipping.example.test/orders/43")

async def orders():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        for url in lookup_urls:
            await client.get(url)
    # Scope exit closes the client.

# Repeated calls with a separate client for each iteration:
async def separate_clients():
    for url in lookup_urls:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            await client.get(url)

annotations.text: One owning scope can reuse an AsyncClient for several awaited lookups, benefiting from connection pooling. Avoid constructing a new client inside a hot loop. Awaiting get or post performs a request; it does not close the client. Close at the end of the owning scope with the async context manager or await client.aclose().

steps.title: Trace the boundary: Async-compatible external HTTP requests

blocks.text: Compare orders() with separate_clients() in the shipping-lookup example. In orders(), the loop sits inside one async with httpx.AsyncClient() scope, so each awaited client.get(url) reuses that client and can benefit from connection pooling. In separate_clients(), client construction sits inside the loop instead. For either layout, distinguish awaiting the request from closing the client: cleanup belongs at the end of the owning scope, through context-manager exit or await client.aclose().

tiles.title: Custom validation for domain invariants · Expected API failures with HTTPException

steps.title: The rule: Custom validation for domain invariants

blocks.text: Choose @model_validator(mode='after') on an instance method to check an invariant involving multiple already-validated fields.

An after-model validator raises ValueError when its invariant fails and returns self when validation succeeds. Use @field_validator('field', mode='after') with a classmethod for a custom check on one validated field, returning the validated value when accepted. Verify a cross-field rule with input that passes each individual field's validation but violates the model invariant, asserting that model construction raises ValidationError; also verify a consistent input is accepted.

annotations.text: For the booking rule, end must be later than start. Use individually valid values that violate that relationship to isolate the invariant. An after-model instance validator raises ValueError on failure; construction then raises ValidationError. A consistent pair succeeds and the validator returns self. For a custom single-field check, use an after-field classmethod validator and return the accepted value.

steps.title: The rule: Expected API failures with HTTPException

blocks.text: Raise HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...) to stop the operation and return a deliberate HTTP rejection rather than returning the exception object.
HTTPException accepts headers for required response metadata, such as an authentication challenge. FastAPI's default HTTPException response contains the supplied detail under the JSON key detail.

At the absent-order branch, raise HTTPException with the intended status and client-facing detail. The raise stops normal operation work and produces a deliberate HTTP rejection; returning the exception object is different. FastAPI puts the supplied detail under the default JSON key detail. Supply headers when the rejection requires metadata, such as an authentication challenge.

tiles.title: Choosing def versus async def from I/O behavior without blocking the event loop

steps.title: The rule: Choosing def versus async def from I/O behavior without blocking the event loop

blocks.text: Choose async def and await for an I/O library with awaitable operations; use a normal def handler for a blocking I/O library.

FastAPI runs a normal def path operation in an external thread pool, whereas an async def path operation runs as asynchronous execution. FastAPI does not automatically move ordinary utility functions called directly by a handler to a thread pool; a blocking call inside async def can block the event loop.

nodes.label: def path operation: external thread pool
async def → directly called blocking utility

edges.label: not automatically offloaded; can block event loop

blocks.alt_text: Make three execution paths visible: an async def handler awaiting an awaitable shipping operation on the event loop; a normal def handler performing blocking shipping I/O in the external thread pool; and an async def handler directly calling a blocking utility that remains on and can block the event loop.

steps.title: Trace the boundary: Choosing def versus async def from I/O behavior without blocking the event loop

blocks.text: Match the handler to the I/O library. Awaitable operations fit async def with await. Blocking I/O fits a normal def path operation, which FastAPI runs in an external thread pool. Moving a blocking call into a directly called helper does not automatically offload it: inside async def, that call can block the event loop.

tiles.title: Modular FastAPI application composition with APIRouter

steps.title: The rule: Modular FastAPI application composition with APIRouter

blocks.text: Create an APIRouter for a feature's operations and register those operations on that router rather than requiring all handlers to live in the main module.

Import feature routers and call app.include_router(router) to assemble their operations into the application. An include_router prefix adds to the included operations' paths, and tags, dependencies and responses can be supplied at inclusion.

blocks.code:
# orders.py
from fastapi import APIRouter
router = APIRouter()
@router.get('/orders')
def list_orders():
    return []

# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
from orders import router
app.include_router(router, prefix='/api')

annotations.text: Register feature operations on an APIRouter, then import and include it in the application assembly module. Defining the router alone does not assemble it. Including a local /orders operation with prefix /api produces /api/orders. The include point can also supply tags, dependencies, and responses.

tiles.title: Typed path and query input binding · Response-model serialization and private-field exclusion

steps.title: The rule: Typed path and query input binding

blocks.text: Put a name in the route path as {name} and declare name: Type in the handler to bind and convert that path value.

Handler parameters not present in the path are interpreted as query parameters when they are ordinary scalar types. A query parameter with a default may be omitted, while a parameter without a default is required; the type controls conversion of a supplied string. A path value that cannot be converted to its declared type produces a validation error instead of invoking the handler with that unconverted value.

annotations.text: In /orders/{order_id}, declare order_id: int to bind and convert the path value. An ordinary scalar limit outside the path binds from the query. A default permits omission; no default makes it required. A nonconvertible path value fails validation instead of reaching the handler unconverted. Source, conversion, and omission are separate decisions.

blocks.text: In /orders/{order_id}, declare order_id: int to bind and convert the path value. An ordinary scalar limit outside the path binds from the query. A default permits omission; no default makes it required. A nonconvertible path value fails validation instead of reaching the handler unconverted. Source, conversion, and omission are separate decisions.

steps.title: Trace the boundary: Typed path and query input binding

blocks.text: Read the read_order signature against /orders/{order_id}. The placeholder supplies order_id, whose int annotation controls conversion; a nonconvertible path value produces a validation error rather than being passed through unchanged. limit has no placeholder, so this ordinary scalar input comes from the query. Its declared default permits omission. Removing that default would make limit required, without changing its query source or the conversion of a supplied string.

steps.title: The rule: Response-model serialization and private-field exclusion

blocks.text: Set response_model=PublicModel on the operation decorator to validate, serialize and filter the returned value to that public model.

Define the output model without private fields so those fields are not returned merely because they exist on the internal object. When both a return annotation and response_model are supplied, response_model takes priority for FastAPI's response processing. Returning a Response object directly bypasses automatic response-model conversion and filtering, so the application is responsible for that content.

annotations.text: PublicOrder lists intended public fields, leaving out the internal private processing note. Set response_model=PublicOrder to validate, serialize, and filter a normally returned value. response_model takes priority over a return annotation. Inspect the return form too: returning a Response directly bypasses automatic model conversion and filtering, leaving its content to the application.

steps.title: The rule: Depends

blocks.text: Declare a handler input with Annotated[Type, Depends(provider)] to have FastAPI execute the provider and supply its returned value.

Pass the provider callable to Depends rather than calling it in the declaration, so FastAPI can resolve its inputs. A dependency makes a handler's needed input explicit and can be reused by multiple operations for shared input-provision logic.

annotations.text: Declare a typed parameter with Annotated[Type, Depends(provider)]. Pass the callable, not provider(). This is an explicit input, not an application-wide hidden value store.

steps.title: The rule: Outbound timeouts

blocks.text: HTTPX distinguishes connect, read, write and pool timeouts; read and write limits bound waiting for individual chunks rather than a whole request's elapsed duration.

Configure a finite timeout with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=seconds) or a request's timeout= argument; timeout=None disables timeout enforcement. HTTPX raises timeout exceptions such as ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout and PoolTimeout when the corresponding wait exceeds its limit. When the contract requires a total elapsed-time budget across asynchronous work, wrap the operation in async with asyncio.timeout(seconds); its cancellation is converted to TimeoutError outside the context.

edges.label: successive chunks: each wait can fit; total can exceed read limit

blocks.alt_text: Make the shipping lookup's connect, pool, read and write wait boundaries visible alongside a separate total elapsed-time boundary. Show that successive chunks can each arrive within the read limit while total elapsed time exceeds that limit, and distinguish HTTPX timeout exceptions from TimeoutError outside asyncio.timeout.

Timely successive chunks can still extend total duration. For a total budget, use async with asyncio.timeout(seconds) and catch TimeoutError outside the context. Keep that separate from HTTPX timeout exceptions; timeout=None disables enforcement.

tiles.title: Separating transport, testable business logic and persistence responsibilities · Bounded in-process background work and nondurable delivery limits · Composing request dependency graphs

steps.title: The rule: Separating transport, testable business logic and persistence responsibilities

blocks.text: A dependency can extract reusable input-provision logic from individual operation handlers and expose the supplied value as a declared handler parameter.

Transport handlers adapt HTTP inputs and outputs, business callables enforce application rules, and persistence adapters access stored state; separate these responsibilities so each can change without embedding the other responsibilities. Move a business decision from a handler into a plain callable with explicit inputs, keep the HTTP adaptation in the handler, and call a separate persistence adapter for stored state rather than treating separate files alone as a responsibility boundary.

edges.label: stored-state access; not embedded in handler

blocks.alt_text: Make the order flow visible across three responsibility boundaries: HTTP adaptation in the handler, the order decision in a plain business callable, and stored-state access in a persistence adapter. Show reusable input provisioning entering through a declared handler parameter, and distinguish responsibility boundaries from file boundaries.

Separate responsibilities, not just files: moving the same mixture into several modules does not establish those boundaries.

steps.title: The rule: Bounded in-process background work and nondurable delivery limits

blocks.text: Declare a BackgroundTasks handler parameter and call background_tasks.add_task(callable, *args, **kwargs) to schedule work after sending the response.

A background task callable can be a normal def or async def function; FastAPI handles either form. BackgroundTasks work runs in the application process and cannot guarantee survival or delivery when that process fails.

steps.title: The rule: Composing request dependency graphs

blocks.text: A provider can declare its own Annotated[Type, Depends(other_provider)] parameter, forming a dependency graph.

FastAPI resolves a provider's prerequisite inputs before calling that provider and supplies its result to the consuming operation. A sub-dependency can declare typed query inputs of its own; those inputs are extracted from the request before its returned value is supplied to the dependent provider.

edges.label: resolve prerequisite and supply its result

blocks.text: The pagination provider declares typed page and page_size query inputs. FastAPI extracts those inputs and resolves pagination before supplying its result to order-options; the consuming operation then receives the order-options result. A provider declares a prerequisite with Annotated[Type, Depends(other_provider)]. Trace from prerequisites toward consumers, not the reverse.

steps.title: The rule: Configuring existing middleware in the request/response stack

blocks.text: The last middleware added is the outermost wrapper: requests traverse it first, while responses traverse it last.

Configure each selected maintained middleware with app.add_middleware(MiddlewareClass, option=value), passing the component's documented options rather than writing its protocol implementation. For two middleware additions, trace the request through the second addition then the first and into the handler, and trace the resulting response through the first addition then the second.

blocks.alt_text: Show the handler nested inside middleware A inside middleware B, label A as the first addition and B as the second, and draw separate request and response arrows in opposite directions.

steps.title: Trace the boundary: Configuring existing middleware in the request/response stack

blocks.text: Add A first and B second with app.add_middleware and each maintained component’s documented options. B is the outermost wrapper. Requests traverse B → A → handler; the resulting response traverses handler → A → B. Addition order explains both directions, but the traversal sequences are not identical. Configure the components rather than implementing their protocols.

steps.title: The rule: Production ASGI serving versus development reload

blocks.text: Run the application with an ASGI server import string, such as uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000, where main names the module and app names its application object.

--reload is useful during development but should not be enabled in production because it consumes resources and is less stable. Uvicorn's --workers option starts multiple worker processes and is mutually exclusive with --reload; choose the worker count for the deployment rather than treating reload as process management.

Use an ASGI server import string: main:app names module main and application object app. The supplied command selects its host and port without reload. --reload is useful in development, but consumes resources and is less stable, so do not enable it in production. --workers starts multiple processes and is mutually exclusive with --reload; choose worker count for the deployment.
